section.title: Salvation for the Foreigner
section.sectionRationale: Having thrown open a free invitation to the thirsty in chapter 55, Isaiah now names exactly who may walk through that door, even the eunuch, barred from the assembly under the law, and the foreigner, once outside the covenant altogether. This is the seam where Isaiah's universal vision of a house of prayer for all nations comes into sharpest focus.
section.thesis: God welcomes the eunuch and the foreigner who hold fast to His covenant and keep His Sabbath, giving them an everlasting name and place in His house, because His house was never meant to be for one people only but a house of prayer for all nations.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the call to justice and Sabbath-keeping as salvation draws near; the eunuch and foreigner told not to count themselves excluded; and God's house declared a house of prayer for all nations.

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “Maintain justice and do what is right, for My salvation is coming soon, and My righteousness will be revealed.
Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds it fast, who keeps the Sabbath without profaning it and keeps his hand from doing any evil.”

units.label: Do not say I am but a dry tree

verses.text: Let no {{nekhar|foreigner}} who has joined himself to the LORD say, “The LORD will utterly exclude me from His people.” And let the {{saris|eunuch}} not say, “I am but a dry tree.”
For this is what the LORD says: “To the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths, who choose what pleases Me and hold fast to My covenant,
I will give them, in My house and within My walls, a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name that will not be cut off.

And the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD to minister to Him, to love the name of the LORD, and to be His servants, all who keep the Sabbath without profaning it and who hold fast to My covenant,

units.label: A house of prayer for all nations

verses.text: I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer. Their burnt offerings and sacrifices will be accepted on My altar, for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations.”
Thus declares the Lord GOD, who gathers the dispersed of Israel: “I will gather to them still others besides those already gathered.”

nekhar.gloss: Foreigner, one from outside Israel's ethnic and covenant boundary. Under the law such a person could be marginal to Israel's worship; here God explicitly welcomes the foreigner who joins himself to the LORD, loves His name, and keeps His covenant, foreshadowing the full inclusion of the nations in Christ.

saris.gloss: Eunuch, a man excluded from full assembly and unable to have descendants, Deuteronomy 23:1. God promises such a man, in His house, a memorial and an everlasting name better than sons and daughters, directly answering his deepest fear of being cut off and forgotten.

basic.context: After inviting all who thirst in chapter 55, Isaiah names two groups the law seemed to shut out, the eunuch, who could not enter the assembly, and the foreigner, outside Israel's covenant people. God tells both plainly not to count themselves excluded; He will give them a place, a name, and joy in His house.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage does not overturn the law lightly, it shows the law's own deeper purpose, a people set apart to display God's holiness so that outsiders could be drawn in, not shut out. Faithful Sabbath-keeping and covenant-holding, not ethnicity or physical wholeness, become the mark of belonging.
basic.originalLanguages: The nekhar, foreigner, and the saris, eunuch, both marginal or barred figures under Israel's law, are here promised full welcome if they hold fast to God's covenant. The eunuch, who could leave no descendants, is given something better, an everlasting name in God's own house.
basic.typology: This anticipates the full inclusion of Gentiles, and of formerly excluded outsiders, into the people of God through Christ, and is fulfilled literally when Philip baptizes the Ethiopian eunuch, himself reading Isaiah, in Acts 8.
basic.christ: Jesus quotes verse 7 directly, my house will be called a house of prayer, when He cleanses the temple, adding the phrase for all nations that the religious leaders had let the court of the Gentiles become a marketplace instead, Mark 11:17. The Ethiopian eunuch of Acts 8, reading Isaiah, becomes a living fulfillment of this very promise, welcomed and baptized though he was exactly the kind of person verse 3 addresses.
basic.god: God's holiness does not exclude the marginal, it welcomes them on the basis of covenant faithfulness rather than physical status or ethnic origin. He is a God who gathers still others besides those already gathered, His house never intended to close its doors.
basic.crossReferences: Mark 11:17 has Jesus quote this passage directly at the temple's cleansing. Acts 8:26-39 shows an actual eunuch, reading Isaiah, welcomed into God's people. Ephesians 2:11-13 describes Gentiles, once far off, brought near by the blood of Christ.
basic.oneStory: From the very people the law seemed to shut out, Isaiah promises a name, a place, and joy in God's own house. That promise becomes flesh in the New Testament when an actual eunuch is baptized and Gentiles are grafted in, proving that God's house was always meant to be a house of prayer for all nations.

context.literary:
Isaiah 56 opens the final section of the book, and it begins with a hinge. The previous chapter ended with a creation that sings and a name that is made for the LORD, Isaiah 55:12-13. Chapter 56 asks what kind of people will belong to that renewed world and who is allowed in. The opening line, 'Maintain justice and do what is right,' sets the terms, and the second half of verse 1 gives the reason: salvation is near and righteousness is about to be revealed.

The passage is built in careful pairs. Verses 1 and 2 state the requirement, justice and the Sabbath, and wrap it in a blessing. Verse 3 then quotes two fearful voices, the foreigner who says, 'The LORD will utterly exclude me,' and the eunuch who says, 'I am but a dry tree.' Verses 4 and 5 answer the eunuch and verses 6 and 7 answer the foreigner, and the two answers run on parallel tracks. Each describes people who keep the Sabbath and hold fast to the covenant, and the same verb, hold fast, appears in verses 2, 4 and 6, binding the section together. Each promise is then given a place, a name in verse 5 and a house in verse 7.

The word 'house' returns three times, 'in My house and within My walls,' verse 5, and 'My house of prayer' twice in verse 7. The word 'name' also recurs, the everlasting name given to the eunuch, and the foreigners who 'love the name of the LORD,' verse 6. Verse 8 closes with a threefold play on gathering, God 'gathers' the dispersed and will 'gather' still others who are not yet 'gathered.' The abrupt shift at verse 9, to beasts of the field and blind watchmen, makes the generosity of the first eight verses stand out against the failure of the leaders.
context.historical:
The world behind this oracle was one of boundaries, and some of them were written into the law. Deuteronomy 23:1 barred a man with crushed or severed genitals from the assembly of the LORD, and Deuteronomy 23:3 kept Ammonites and Moabites out for ten generations. Leviticus 21 also excluded priests with physical defects from approaching the altar. How far these rules reached is debated, since 'the assembly' may describe the gathered community in particular settings and not the right to worship, but eunuchs and foreigners clearly knew themselves to be marked as outsiders.

Eunuchs were not a fringe group in the ancient Near East. The Hebrew word saris could mean a court official and was used of royal servants, and a eunuch might hold high office. The prophet had once told King Hezekiah that some of his descendants would be taken to Babylon to be eunuchs in the palace of its king, Isaiah 39:7. For the exiles this was not an abstract category. Their own sons might become such men, men who would never have children of their own and who, in a culture that measured a family by its heirs, would have no one to carry their name.

Foreigners were also a pressing concern. After the return from exile the community was small and anxious. Ezra and Nehemiah record vigorous efforts to preserve its separateness, including sending away foreign wives and excluding people of foreign descent when the Law was read, Ezra 10:2-3 and Nehemiah 13:1-3. Ezekiel had said that no foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh might enter the sanctuary, Ezekiel 44:9. Isaiah 56 speaks into that mood. It does not remove the call for covenant faithfulness, but it insists that the door is not shut to those who give themselves to the LORD.

The Sabbath mattered more in this setting than it might seem. In exile, without a temple, it was one of the clearest marks of belonging to God's people, a 'sign' between the LORD and Israel, Exodus 31:13-17.
context.canonical:
The welcome of this chapter has roots in the earlier law and is repeated across the prophets. The same statute was to apply to the native and the foreigner who joined Israel in worship, Numbers 15:14-16, and the foreigner could keep the Passover, Exodus 12:48-49. In his prayer at the temple's dedication, Solomon asked the LORD to answer the foreigner who came from a distant land and prayed toward the house, so that all the peoples would know His name, 1 Kings 8:41-43. Psalm 87 pictures the nations being registered as born in Zion.

Isaiah himself has been working toward this. Earlier the foreigner will 'join' Jacob, Isaiah 14:1, and the nations will stream to the mountain of the LORD, Isaiah 2:2-3. Later the book will go further than chapter 56, for the LORD promises to take some of the gathered nations as priests and Levites, Isaiah 66:18-21. Zechariah sees ten men from the nations take hold of a Jew's robe, saying, 'Let us go with you,' Zechariah 8:23.

In the New Testament, Jesus joins verse 7 to Jeremiah 7:11 when He drives out the traders, Mark 11:17. Mark alone keeps the closing words 'for all the nations.' An Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah is baptized in Acts 8:26-39. Peter later understands that God 'welcomes those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right,' Acts 10:34-35. Paul tells Gentile believers they are 'no longer strangers and foreigners,' Ephesians 2:19, and John sees a multitude from every nation standing before the throne, Revelation 7:9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet is addressing two groups in the same breath, and he meant both to listen. The first is the community that was tempted to guard its borders. For them the opening commands are a reminder that salvation is coming and that the people it belongs to must be marked by justice and by honoring the Sabbath, not by pedigree or physical wholeness. The covenant was never a membership of bloodlines alone, and the law's own provisions for resident foreigners show that it was open from the beginning.

The second group is the ones who feared they were shut out. The prophet quotes their inner speech, 'The LORD will utterly exclude me' and 'I am but a dry tree,' and tells them not to say it. He assumes they have already joined themselves to the LORD, so he is not inviting indifference but commending real commitment, and he gives them promises designed to meet the particular wound. The eunuch worried about a name that would vanish is promised a better one. The foreigner worried about a place is promised altar and mountain.

He meant the people to see that the house where God is worshiped belongs to God, who calls it 'My house,' and that the gathering He is doing is bigger than they imagined, verse 8. The result is meant to be a community which does justice, welcomes the outsider, and expects more to come.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter begins with commands and moves to promises, and it is worth keeping the two apart. Verses 1 and 2 are prescriptive: maintain justice, do what is right, keep the Sabbath, and keep the hand from evil. Verses 3 to 8 describe what God will do for people who do this and who hold fast to His covenant. The promise is not a reward earned by keeping the Sabbath, since it is the covenant that brings the person in, and the Sabbath and justice are the way belonging looks in practice.

Several applications need care. Verse 7 does not abolish the distinction between those who belong to the covenant and those who do not, and it does not settle questions of national borders or immigration. It speaks of people who 'join themselves to the LORD.' It is about welcome into the worshiping people of God, not about every public policy concerning foreigners. Nor is the eunuch a symbol for every kind of marginalization. He is a specific person who was excluded by specific rules, and the principle that follows is that no one barred by the old boundaries is barred by God's grace.

The Sabbath is a particular case. Christians have understood it in different ways, from keeping a weekly day of rest and worship to seeing its fulfillment in the rest given in Christ, Hebrews 4:9-10, Mark 2:27-28. The passage itself does not settle that question, and it should not be used as a blunt tool against believers who differ.

debates.question: How does Isaiah 56:3-8 relate to the exclusions in Deuteronomy 23:1-3 and Ezekiel 44:9?

views.label: Isaiah overrides the earlier law
views.case: Deuteronomy 23:1 says a man with crushed or severed genitals may not enter the assembly, and Isaiah promises the eunuch a name in God's house. Some read this as a prophetic revision that sets aside a law of an earlier era, with a more generous covenant replacing a more restricted one.

views.label: Isaiah draws out what the law already allowed
views.case: The law had provisions for resident foreigners, Numbers 15:14-16, and Solomon's prayer expects foreigners to pray at the temple, 1 Kings 8:41-43. Isaiah, on this view, is applying the generosity already in the law to those whom a strict reading had left in doubt. Ezekiel 44:9 excludes foreigners 'uncircumcised in heart and flesh,' which targets those who show no commitment, not all foreigners.

views.label: A new situation in the age of salvation
views.case: Verse 1 says that God's salvation is about to come and His righteousness to be revealed. The relaxation of the barrier belongs to that new moment. The old rules were real, but they were given for a time when the way into God's presence was guarded, and the arrival of salvation changes what that guard means.

debates.bearing: Whichever route is taken, the text gives the same answer to the question 'Am I shut out?' The old boundaries were never a verdict on a person's worth or on God's heart, and the New Testament sees them removed in Christ, Ephesians 2:14-19.

debates.question: What is the service of the foreigners in verse 6, 'to minister to Him'?

views.label: Ordinary worship by lay worshipers
views.case: The verse speaks of foreigners who love the name, keep the Sabbath, and whose offerings are accepted on the altar. This is the life of faithful worshipers, who bring sacrifices and pray in the house, and nothing in verse 7 requires priestly office.

views.label: Priestly service
views.case: The verb used for 'minister' is the one used of those who serve in the sanctuary. Later in the book God promises to select some of the nations as priests and Levites, Isaiah 66:21, and Isaiah 61:6 calls Israel the priests of the LORD. So the foreigners may be pictured as sharing in actual sacred service.

views.label: A staged promise
views.case: Verses 6 and 7 may describe the beginning of inclusion, in which the foreigner is welcomed as a worshiper, and Isaiah 66:21 shows where it ends. The passage is one step on a path.

debates.bearing: The New Testament reads the fulfillment in terms of the priesthood of all believers, 1 Peter 2:5 and 2:9, in which Jew and Gentile alike offer spiritual sacrifices. That fits a staged reading in which the promise grows from welcome to service.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 says the foreigner has 'joined himself' to the LORD. The Hebrew verb behind this, from the root lavah, means to be attached or joined, and it carries a particular memory. Leah gave her third son the name Levi because she hoped her husband would become 'attached' to her, Genesis 29:34. In Numbers 18:2 and 18:4 the Levites are to 'join' Aaron and his sons in the work of the Tent, using the same root, while 'no outsider may come near.' Isaiah gives the foreigner the vocabulary of the Levite. The one who was outside the Tent is described by the very verb that described those closest to it.

The eunuch's lament, 'I am but a dry tree,' uses ets yavesh. The picture is of a tree with no sap, which will leave no fruit and no seed. The LORD can reverse that picture, as in Ezekiel 17:24, where He says He makes 'the withered tree flourish.' Isaiah does not promise the eunuch children. He promises something that answers the fear behind the lament.

In verse 5 the gift is 'a memorial and a name,' in Hebrew yad vashem, literally 'a hand and a name.' The word yad can mean a monument or pillar. Absalom, who had no son to preserve his name, set up a pillar called 'Absalom's Monument,' 2 Samuel 18:18, using the same word. The eunuch is promised a memorial that outlasts a stone one, within God's own walls. The modern memorial in Jerusalem draws its name from this verse.

The verbs of keeping run through the passage. Verse 1 opens with 'maintain,' from the common verb shamar, to keep or guard, and the same verb describes keeping the Sabbath in verses 2, 4 and 6. The commands about justice and the Sabbath are one action of guarding. Alongside it, chazaq, to hold fast, in verses 2, 4 and 6 gives the other half of faithfulness: not only watching over what God has said but gripping it.

Finally, in verse 7 the house will be called beit tefillah, a house of prayer. The Septuagint renders it with Greek words for a house of prayer, and Jesus quotes it that way in the Gospels. The phrase 'for all the nations' appears in Mark 11:17 and not in Matthew 21:13 or Luke 19:46, so Mark preserves the clause that most directly states Isaiah's scope. The Hebrew word 'accepted' in the same verse, ratson, is the language of sacrifice that pleases God, so the foreigner's offering is not tolerated but welcomed.

typology.type: The eunuch who is given a name and a future, verses 4 and 5
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's promise is answered by a story in Acts 8. An Ethiopian official, a eunuch, is reading Isaiah as he rides home from Jerusalem, and the passage he is on is Isaiah 53, 'who can recount His descendants?' Acts 8:32-33. The Servant is himself 'cut off from the land of the living,' Isaiah 53:8, and yet is promised that He 'will see His offspring,' Isaiah 53:10. The eunuch reads of One who seemed childless and who will have a family, and is baptized into it, Acts 8:36-38. The type falls short only in this: Isaiah promised a name within the temple walls, and the reality is a place in the household of God.

typology.type: The foreigner brought near to God's mountain, verses 6 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The nations joining themselves to the LORD are fulfilled in the Gentile believers whom Paul addresses as once 'alienated from the commonwealth of Israel' and now 'fellow citizens with the saints,' Ephesians 2:12 and 2:19. Jesus Himself points to it when He says many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Matthew 8:11. Matthew's genealogy even names two foreign women, Rahab and Ruth, among the ancestors of the Messiah, Matthew 1:5. The type falls short because the mountain of Isaiah is a place, while the New Testament places believers in a person.

typology.type: A house of prayer for all the nations, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The temple was built to be the place where nations could pray, and Jesus acts to defend that purpose, Mark 11:17. He also says the temple is His body, John 2:19-21, and the apostles describe believers as living stones being built into a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:5, with Christ as the cornerstone, Ephesians 2:20-22. The correspondence is that the house becomes a people, with the Gentiles included. The type falls short because Isaiah pictures sacrifices on an altar, and the sacrifices of the new house are praise and lives given to God, Hebrews 13:15.

typology.type: The Sabbath as the mark of belonging, verses 2, 4 and 6
typology.fulfillment: The Sabbath was a sign of the covenant, and Isaiah makes it the thing the outsider can share. In the New Testament Jesus declares Himself Lord of the Sabbath, Mark 2:28, and invites the weary to come to Him for rest, Matthew 11:28. Hebrews says a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9-10, and Paul calls the Sabbath a shadow whose body belongs to Christ, Colossians 2:16-17. The type falls short because the weekly day only points toward a rest that Christ gives in full.

typology.type: Others gathered besides those already gathered, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: Jesus says almost the same words about His own mission: 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well,' John 10:16. The aim is one flock and one shepherd. Isaiah's gathering of the dispersed is the work of the good Shepherd, and the nations are the sheep not yet in the fold. The vision is completed in Revelation 7:9. The type falls short in that Isaiah speaks of a gathering to a mountain, whereas Jesus speaks of a gathering to Himself.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most clearly by His own use of verse 7. When Jesus overturns the tables and says, 'Is it not written: My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations?' Mark 11:17, He is not making a general point about reverence. He is defending the place that Isaiah promised to foreigners. The traders were operating in the part of the temple where the nations could pray, and by filling it with commerce the leaders had blocked the very promise of Isaiah 56:7. Jesus joins the verse to Jeremiah's charge of a den of robbers, Jeremiah 7:11, because both prophets saw a house that had been made to serve its keepers.

It leads to Christ through the Servant who makes a family for the childless. In Acts 8 the eunuch is reading Isaiah 53, a few chapters back from our passage, and Philip 'began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus,' Acts 8:35. The One who was cut off from the land of the living, Isaiah 53:8, and who died without descendants, is the One who 'will see His offspring,' Isaiah 53:10. The eunuch, who stood for the man whose name would end, finds that the Servant's death opens a name for him. Jesus Himself speaks of those who live as eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, Matthew 19:12, and does not treat that condition as a mark of exclusion.

It leads to Christ in the way He draws the nations. A centurion's faith astonishes Him, and He says many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet, Matthew 8:10-11. Some Greeks go up to worship at the feast and ask to see Him, John 12:20-21. He says of His sheep, 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well,' John 10:16, which is Isaiah 56:8 in His own voice.

The cross is the price of this inclusion. The wall that kept foreigners from the inner courts becomes, in Paul's picture, the 'dividing wall of hostility' that Christ tore down, and He did it 'by abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees' so as to make one new man of two, Ephesians 2:14-15. In Him both Jew and Gentile have 'access to the Father by one Spirit,' Ephesians 2:18. The offering that is 'accepted on My altar' in Isaiah 56:7 is now brought through Jesus, who is the way into the presence, Hebrews 13:15.

A caution is in order. The Ethiopian is a real person and his baptism is a real event, but the passage does not turn every detail into a code. Isaiah's words are addressed to the eunuchs and foreigners of his own day, and the New Testament shows how the pattern continues, not that each verse has one hidden meaning. What can be said is that Jesus is the one who fulfills Isaiah's promise to the outsiders and who throws the doors open for them to come in.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the God of a house that is truly His. He calls it 'My house' and 'My holy mountain' and 'My altar,' and these possessives matter. The temple is not the property of a family, a tribe or a class. Since it is His, He decides who is welcome, and He announces that the welcome is wider than any of His people had thought. This is a God who does not accept that His own people may close a door He has opened.

He is a God who hears the unspoken thoughts of the people He loves. Verse 3 quotes things that the foreigner and the eunuch say to themselves, and God does not leave them to say them. He answers a fear that had not been voiced to anyone. The same God who knows the heart, as Peter later says, Acts 15:8, sees through every credential to the person inside.

He is generous in the specific way that heals the wound. The eunuch fears the loss of a name, and God offers a better one than sons and daughters, which no one can cut off. The foreigner fears being kept apart, and God brings him to the holy mountain and makes him joyful in the house of prayer. He does not give a generic blessing. He matches each person's worst fear with the specific gift that answers it, which is how a good Father gives.

He holds covenant standards and welcome together. The people who are welcomed are those who keep the Sabbath, hold fast to the covenant and love the name. The standard does not shrink to let people in, and the welcome is not conditional on rank. Holiness and hospitality are not opposites, because the boundaries of the law were given to guard worship, not to deny love.

He is also a gatherer. The end of the passage names Him as the One 'who gathers the dispersed of Israel,' and promises 'still others.' It is part of His character to collect what was scattered, as the shepherd of Isaiah 40:11 gathers lambs in his arms. His saving work is not exhausted by the people already in view.

For worship, the passage teaches us to come to God's house as guests of a host who has made room, and to make sure the house we keep is open to the one whom He welcomes. It rebukes any practice of worship that treats a place at the table as a possession, and it invites anyone who fears being left out to hear God say, in answer to the unspoken question, that He has already made a place.

crossReferences.note: The law barred the man with crushed genitals, and Ammonites and Moabites, from the assembly of the LORD. These are the rules the eunuch and foreigner of Isaiah 56 would have known. The prophet does not hide the earlier law, and his promise is aimed directly at the people it appeared to shut out.

The foreigner residing with Israel who wants to make an offering to the LORD is to do exactly as the native does, under the same statute. Isaiah 56:6-7 is not a new idea. The law already provided for foreigners to worship, and the prophet declares that this is what God always intended.

At the dedication of the temple Solomon asks God to answer the foreigner who comes from a distant land and prays toward it, so that all peoples will know His name. This is the first stated purpose of the temple for the nations, and Isaiah 56:7 gathers it into a title, a house of prayer for all the nations.

Isaiah tells Hezekiah that some of his descendants will be taken to be eunuchs in the palace of Babylon's king. The royal line itself would produce eunuchs. When Isaiah 56 promises the eunuch an everlasting name, he is speaking to a group that his own earlier oracle had said would include David's family.

The Servant is cut off from the land of the living and asked, 'who can recount His descendants?' Yet He will see His offspring. The eunuch of Acts 8 is reading this passage, and the Servant's story gives the childless a family, which explains why Isaiah 56 can speak of a name better than sons.

The book's closing chapter goes beyond chapter 56. God will gather all nations to see His glory, send survivors to those who have not heard His fame, and take some of them as priests and Levites. It shows where the welcome of Isaiah 56:6-7 was always headed.

Jesus drives out the traders and quotes verse 7 with its final clause, 'for all the nations.' Mark preserves the phrase that Matthew and Luke omit. The traders filled the outer courts, where foreigners could pray, which is why His action is a defense of Isaiah's promise.

An Ethiopian official in charge of a queen's treasury, a eunuch who had gone to Jerusalem to worship, reads Isaiah, hears the good news and asks what prevents his baptism. The answer is nothing. The man Isaiah 56:3 names is brought into the people of God in the next generation.

Paul tells Gentiles that they were once strangers to the covenants, but that Christ has torn down the dividing wall and made one new man of two. They are now fellow citizens and members of God's household. It is Isaiah 56 explained, with the cross as the way the foreigner is brought near.

Jesus says He has other sheep not of this fold, and that He must bring them in. It echoes Isaiah 56:8, 'still others besides those already gathered,' and makes the gathering the work of the Shepherd Himself, with the aim of one flock and one shepherd.

Many peoples and strong nations will come to seek the LORD in Jerusalem, and ten men will grasp the robe of a Jew, saying, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.' It is a vivid picture of Isaiah 56:6-7 from the viewpoint of those who come.

John sees a multitude too large to count from every nation, tribe, people and tongue, standing before the throne and the Lamb. This is the final form of the gathering in Isaiah 56:8, the house of prayer for all the nations filled at last.

study.oneStory:
From Genesis 12 the Bible has two movements side by side. God sets apart one family, and He says through that family all the families of the earth will be blessed. The setting apart produced boundaries, such as the rules of Deuteronomy 23, the Sabbath that marked Israel, and the walls and courts of the temple. The blessing of the nations produced a steady counter-pressure. A foreigner could join Israel at the Passover, Ruth the Moabite became the great-grandmother of David, Solomon prayed for the stranger, and the prophets saw the nations climbing to the mountain.

Isaiah 56 is a moment where the second movement leans hard on the first. The scattered people of God, coming home from exile with their anxieties about purity, hear that the door does not close behind them. Anyone who joins himself to the LORD, even those the law had marked as outsiders, may enter. The chapter is a bridge from the Abrahamic promise to the Gentile mission.

The story after it moves quickly in the Gospels and Acts. Jesus claims the temple as a house of prayer for all nations. The Spirit falls on Gentiles in Caesarea, and Peter concludes that God makes no distinction between them and the Jewish believers, Acts 15:8-9. A eunuch from the edge of the known world goes home rejoicing. The apostles argue about whether the Gentiles must keep the law, and they conclude that they are saved by grace, as the Jews are.

The end is a scene that fulfills verse 8 on the scale Isaiah hints at. Revelation pictures people from every nation standing before the Lamb, Revelation 7:9. The seer also hears that the dwelling of God is with man, and that He will dwell with them, Revelation 21:3. The eunuch who feared he was a dry tree and the foreigner who feared he would be excluded find there what God promised through Isaiah, a place within the walls, a name that is not cut off and a house that is never closed. The boundary of the garden, where cherubim kept sinners out, is replaced by a city whose gates are never shut.

quiz.q: What does God promise to the eunuch who keeps His Sabbaths and holds fast to His covenant?

options.text: A memorial and an everlasting name in God's house, better than sons and daughters.
options.note: Verse 5 directly answers the eunuch's fear of being cut off without descendants.

options.text: Physical healing so he is no longer a eunuch.
options.note: This addresses his real condition, but the promise given is a name and place in God's house, not a physical change.

options.text: Exclusion from the assembly, matching Deuteronomy's restriction.
options.note: The passage reverses this expectation, promising full welcome.

options.text: A temporary place outside the temple courts.
options.note: The promise is to be within God's house and walls, not kept at a distance.

quiz.q: How does Jesus use Isaiah 56:7 in the Gospels?

options.text: He quotes it while cleansing the temple, rebuking leaders for turning a house of prayer for all nations into a marketplace.
He quotes it to explain a parable about seeds.
options.note: It is quoted specifically at the temple cleansing.

options.text: He uses it to argue foreigners should never enter the temple.
options.note: This is the opposite of Jesus' point; He emphasizes the phrase for all nations to rebuke exclusion, not enforce it.

options.text: It is never quoted in the Gospels.

quiz.q: What qualification does the passage give for the foreigner's welcome into God's house?

options.text: Joining himself to the LORD, loving His name, and keeping His covenant and Sabbath, not ethnicity.
options.note: Verses 3-6 describe covenant faithfulness as the qualifying mark, not birth.

options.text: First becoming ethnically Israelite through marriage.
options.note: The text names covenant faithfulness, not ethnic assimilation, as the mark of belonging.

options.text: Bringing enough wealth to the temple treasury.
options.note: The passage speaks of loving the LORD's name and covenant faithfulness as the qualification, not wealth brought to the treasury.

options.text: No qualification is given; all foreigners are welcomed unconditionally regardless of belief.
options.note: The passage does specify conditions, joining himself to the LORD and holding fast to His covenant.

quiz.q: What event in Acts embodies the promise of Isaiah 56:3-5?

options.text: Philip's encounter with the Ethiopian eunuch, who is reading Isaiah and is baptized.
options.note: Acts 8:26-39 is a striking, literal fulfillment of the eunuch's welcome promised here.

options.text: Peter's vision of the sheet of animals in Acts 10.
options.note: That passage concerns clean and unclean food and Gentile inclusion generally, but Acts 8's eunuch is the direct fulfillment of this specific promise.

options.text: The stoning of Stephen in Acts 7.
options.note: That event is unrelated to the eunuch and foreigner promise of Isaiah 56.

options.text: Paul's shipwreck on Malta in Acts 27.
options.note: Unrelated to this passage's specific promise.

questions: The eunuch feared being called a dry tree, cut off with no future. What fear of being excluded or forgotten do you carry that God is inviting you to bring to Him?
God's welcome here is tied to genuinely holding fast to His covenant, not merely proximity to His people. Is your own faith a matter of genuine covenant devotion, or mostly cultural belonging?
Jesus quoted this passage to rebuke a temple that had crowded out the very people it was meant to welcome. Where might you be, even unintentionally, making it harder for an outsider to approach God?
God says He will gather still others besides those already gathered, verse 8. Who is someone outside your usual circle that God might be calling you to welcome or reach out to?
The eunuch was promised something better than sons and daughters, a name in God's own house. Where are you tempted to measure your worth by what you lack rather than by your place in God's family?

translationNotes.note: Blessed is the man, and the son of man, uses inclusive Hebrew idiom for humanity generally, not a title for a specific figure, distinct from the later apocalyptic use of son of man.
Dry tree renders a Hebrew idiom for one who leaves no descendants, capturing the eunuch's particular grief under the old covenant's expectations of family lineage.
